parts.title: Campus Conversation: Applying for a Study Abroad Program
script: Narrator
Listen to a conversation between a student and an advisor at the study abroad office.
Student
Hi, I'm interested in studying abroad next fall. Can you tell me how to apply?
Advisor
Of course. First, you need to fill out an online application. The deadline is March fifteenth.
Student
March fifteenth? That's earlier than I expected. Do I need anything else besides the form?
Advisor
Yes. You need a letter from one of your professors, and your grade point average must be at least three point zero.
Student
My average is three point two, so that should be fine. Which countries can I choose?
Advisor
We have partner universities in Spain, Japan, and Australia. Many students choose Spain because the cost of living is lower.
Student
I'd love to improve my Spanish, but I'm worried about money. Is there any financial help?
Advisor
Yes, there are scholarships. You can apply for one at the same time. Students usually get a decision in April.
Student
That's good news. Could you say again what I need to bring to the application?
Advisor
Sure. Just the professor's letter. Everything else is online, and I can email you the link today.
Student
Great. I'll ask Professor Baker for a letter this week. Thank you so much for your help!
Advisor
You're welcome. Start early, because professors are busy in March.
Narrator
Now get ready to answer the questions.
Narrator
Listen again to part of the conversation. Then answer the question.
Advisor
Sure. Just the professor's letter. Everything else is online, and I can email you the link today.

parts.title: Biology Lecture: How Coral Reefs Form
script: Narrator
Listen to part of a lecture in a biology class.
Professor
Today we will talk about coral reefs. Many people think coral is a plant or a rock. But coral is actually an animal.
Professor
A single coral animal is called a polyp. It is very small, only a few millimeters wide. Polyps live together in huge groups.
Professor
Each polyp makes a hard skeleton from calcium in the sea water. When polyps die, their skeletons stay. New polyps grow on top. Over thousands of years, this builds a reef.
Professor
Now, corals have a special partner. Tiny algae live inside the coral. The algae use sunlight to make food, and they share this food with the coral. In return, the coral gives the algae a safe home.
Professor
Because the algae need sunlight, reefs only grow in shallow, clear water. Most reefs are also in warm water, between twenty and thirty degrees Celsius.
Professor
Why do reefs matter? Although they cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, about one quarter of all sea animals live in or near them. Reefs also protect coasts from strong waves.
Professor
Sadly, reefs are in danger. When the water becomes too warm, the coral pushes out the algae. The coral turns white. This is called bleaching. Without the algae, the coral can starve.
Professor
So, scientists are trying to protect reefs by studying how to keep the water cooler and cleaner.
Narrator
Now get ready to answer the questions.
Narrator
Listen again to part of the lecture. Then answer the question.
Professor
Because the algae need sunlight, reefs only grow in shallow, clear water.

questions.q: What is the lecture mainly about?
o: How coral reefs form and why they matter
How to travel to the ocean
questions.exp: The professor explains how reefs form and why they are important.

o: To explain where reefs can grow
To describe how deep the ocean is
To say reefs are not important
To start a new topic about fish
questions.exp: He explains the condition that limits reef growth.

o: It is caused by water that is too warm
It is caused by too much sunlight
questions.exp: Bleaching happens when the water becomes too warm.
